I’ve been struggling at work for maybe the past year or so, but it’s gotten more noticeable in the last few months. As an editor I’m supposed to keep track of timelines, multiple cuts, notes from directors, and different versions, and I keep losing the thread. I’ll open a project intending to do one specific change, and then jump to something else on the timeline or another sequence and forget what I was doing in the first place. My desktop and project bins are a mess; I keep telling myself I’ll organize them, but I get overwhelmed and put it off.

In the studio, I can’t seem to sit still for long. I’m always bouncing my leg, getting up to pace, going to grab coffee, then water, then checking something on my phone. Even when I’m at home watching something, I’m shifting around or getting up mid-episode. People at work have joked that once I start talking in reviews or over lunch, I kind of go on and on and it’s hard for me to dial it back.

I also feel pretty keyed up most days—tense, kind of on edge—and my mind jumps around a lot, which makes it even harder to focus, but I’m not totally sure what’s driving what.
D001-D011_h001.question_a:
I cut film for a living, so my whole job is about focusing, but that’s exactly what I can’t seem to do. I’ll be halfway through a scene and a notification pops up, or someone walks past the door, or I suddenly think of a different project, and I’m just gone. Even if it’s silent, my own thoughts jump to some random idea I “have” to check right then. I keep starting timelines, folders, color passes, and then abandoning them. My desktop is a mess; I’m always losing track of versions and deadlines.

People at work joke that I never sit still. Even when I’m in the edit bay, I’m bouncing my leg, spinning in the chair, getting up to pace for no real reason. It doesn’t feel like worry—it’s just this buzz, like I’m wired. I talk a lot too; I’ll start chatting about some new camera trick or movie I saw and steamroll meetings.

I’ve been like this since at least elementary school—teachers were always telling me to stay in my seat and stop talking. The anxiety feels more recent, mostly about work and money, but the fidgeting and distractedness were there long before I started feeling anxious.
D001-D011_h001.question_b:
I’ve been anxious pretty much all the time for at least the last year and a half. It’s like my brain never shuts up—constantly running through worst‑case scenarios about work, money, my health, my family. When I’m trying to cut a scene, I’ll catch myself replaying conversations, worrying I’ve messed something up, or thinking about deadlines and how the director might hate my edit. Then I realize I’ve been staring at the same frame for ten minutes, totally lost in my head.

I used to be pretty organized with projects, but now I struggle to keep track of versions, notes, and timelines because my mind drifts into “what if” spirals. It’s less that something around me distracts me and more that my own worrying thoughts pull me away from what I’m doing.

Physically I feel keyed up, like I’m running on nervous energy. Even when I’m sitting in the editing bay, I’m bouncing my leg or pacing during renders, almost like I’m propelled by the anxiety itself. D001-D011_h023.question_both:
I’ve been having a really hard time focusing, especially at work. I’ll be coding and I’ll miss really obvious bugs or forget to handle basic edge cases, even after reviewing my own code a couple of times. My pull requests keep coming back with comments about “careless mistakes,” which is embarrassing because I don’t feel like I’m being sloppy on purpose.

My manager will give me a task, and I understand it in the moment, but I’ll either only half-finish it or jump to something else before it’s done. Then I end up scrambling right before deadlines. It’s similar at home—laundry half done, dishes soaking for days. It’s like I lose the thread midway through.

I also feel like I can’t sit still. Even in long meetings or when I’m hanging out with friends, I’m bouncing my leg, checking my phone, getting up to pace. People joke that I’m “powered by caffeine,” but I’m like this even without coffee. I catch myself cutting people off in conversations or finishing their sentences because I get impatient waiting, and then I realize I’ve talked over them. This has all been going on for at least the last couple of years, and it feels like it’s getting more noticeable.
D001-D011_h023.question_a:
I’ve always been kind of scattered, even as a kid. Teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but “easily distracted” and never finished my worksheets. That’s pretty much followed me into my job now. I’ll be working on a feature and then an email pops up, or I overhear something in the office, and suddenly I’m down a rabbit hole reading documentation for some new framework instead of finishing what I started. I make stupid mistakes in my code—missing semicolons, wrong variables—things I know, but I just skim instead of really checking.

My manager gives me clear tasks, and I genuinely mean to follow through, but I’ll jump to the next “interesting” thing before I’m done. At home it’s the same—half-assembled furniture, laundry half-folded.

Physically, I feel like I’m always revved up. Even when I’m just sitting in a meeting, my leg is bouncing, I’m fiddling with a pen, wanting it to end so I can move. I talk over people without meaning to, cut into conversations, answer questions before others finish.

I do feel anxious at times—like, I worry I’ll mess up at work—but the restlessness and jumping around happens even when I’m not actively worrying about anything. It’s more like my brain is constantly chasing the next thing that grabs my attention.
D001-D011_h023.question_b:
Honestly, my mind just never shuts off. I’m constantly running through worst‑case scenarios—bugs I might have missed in my code, getting fired, my parents getting sick, even random disasters. It’s been like this pretty much every day for at least the past year.

At work, I’ve started missing really obvious things in my code reviews—typos, wrong variables—stuff I know how to catch. It’s not that I’m bored or distracted by things around me; I’ll be staring straight at the screen, but my brain is replaying some meeting or worrying about an upcoming deadline. I’ll read the same line of code three or four times and still not take it in because I’m stuck in my head.

My manager has mentioned I don’t always finish tickets on time. It’s usually because I get wrapped up in second‑guessing everything—what if this breaks production, what if I missed an edge case—so I stall or restart tasks.

Physically I feel wired all the time, like I’ve had too much coffee even when I haven’t. I’m fidgety in meetings, bouncing my leg, getting up to pace. I’ll jump into conversations or cut people off, not because I’m excited, but because I’m so tense and afraid I’ll forget a point or they’ll think I don’t know what I’m doing.
